items.value: Statements I and III only are correct — an Ordinance can amend a Central Act and can be given retrospective effect, but it cannot abridge a Fundamental Right
items.reasoning: Under Article 123(2) an Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, so it can amend, modify or repeal any Central Act — statement I is correct. Like an Act, it can also be made retrospective and given effect from a back date — statement III is correct. Statement II fails because Article 123(3) makes void any Ordinance provision that Parliament itself could not have enacted, and Article 13 bars Parliament from making a law that takes away or abridges a Fundamental Right; so an Ordinance cannot abridge one either.

items.value: Only two pairs are correctly matched — Arunachal Pradesh and Tripura; Nagaland was created by an ordinary Act of Parliament, not a Constitutional Amendment Act
items.reasoning: Pair I is correct: Itanagar is named after the Ita Fort ('fort of bricks') and Arunachal Pradesh has exactly two National Parks, Namdapha and Mouling. Pair III is correct: Tripura was a Part 'C' State in 1950, became a centrally administered Union Territory when Part 'C' States were abolished in the 1956 reorganisation, and attained full statehood in 1972. Pair II is the doubtful one and is taken as incorrect: Nagaland was brought into existence by the State of Nagaland Act, 1962 — a law made under Article 3 — and Article 4 expressly says such a law is not to be deemed an amendment of the Constitution; the Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1962 only inserted Article 371A conferring special provisions. The state actually created BY a Constitutional Amendment is Sikkim (36th Amendment, 1975). Note that some standard texts loosely credit the 13th Amendment with Nagaland's statehood, which is why this pair is genuinely contestable.

items.value: Only one — the Inter-State Council is the sole constitutional body among the three
items.reasoning: The Inter-State Council was set up in 1990 by a Presidential order issued under Article 263, which expressly empowers the President to establish such a council — so it is established as per a provision of the Constitution. The National Security Council was created in 1998 by an executive resolution of the Government and has no constitutional or even statutory basis. The Zonal Councils are statutory bodies created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (the North-Eastern Council came later by a separate Act of 1971), not by the Constitution.

items.value: Statement I only — the Constitution does explicitly provide for the Governor's discretion, but the President cannot reserve a State bill on his own
items.reasoning: Statement I is correct: Article 163(1) itself carves out functions the Governor is 'by or under this Constitution required to exercise in his discretion', and explicit discretionary spheres appear in Article 371A (Nagaland, law and order), Paragraph 9(2) of the Sixth Schedule, and Article 239(2) where a Governor acts as administrator of a Union Territory. Statement II is wrong: under Articles 200 and 201 the route to the President runs only through the Governor, who alone may reserve a State bill for the President's consideration; the President has no power to reach out and reserve a State bill suo motu.

items.value: All three pairs are correctly matched
items.reasoning: Separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State is Article 50, which sits in Part IV, the Directive Principles — pair I is right. Valuing and preserving the rich heritage of our composite culture is Article 51A(f), a Fundamental Duty in Part IVA — pair II is right. Prohibition of employment of children below fourteen in any factory or mine is Article 24, a Fundamental Right in Part III (Right against Exploitation) — pair III is right.

items.value: Neither statement is correct
items.reasoning: Statement I is wrong: declaring an area a Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule does not strip the State of its executive power. The State's executive power continues to extend to the area; what changes is that the Governor acquires special responsibilities — he may direct that a Parliamentary or State law shall not apply or shall apply with modifications, may make regulations, and must be advised by a Tribes Advisory Council. No local body assumes 'total administration'. Statement II is also wrong: Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule requires the Governor to report annually (or when required) to the President, and extends the executive power of the Union only to the GIVING OF DIRECTIONS to the State about administering such areas. Giving directions is not taking over the total administration, and the Fifth Schedule contains no takeover provision triggered by a Governor's recommendation.

items.value: None of the pairs is correctly matched — the three ministries have been cyclically swapped
items.reasoning: The National Automotive Board comes under the Ministry of Heavy Industries (Department of Heavy Industry), not Commerce and Industry. The Coir Board is a statutory body under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, not Heavy Industries. The National Centre for Trade Information, a joint venture of India Trade Promotion Organisation and NIC, comes under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not MSME. The three correct ministries are exactly the three printed, rotated by one position, which is the design tell that every pair is deliberately mismatched.

items.value: Subjects I and II only — the Seventh Schedule Lists and Article 162 need State ratification; the conditions of the Governor's office do not
items.reasoning: The proviso to Article 368(2) lists exhaustively what needs ratification by at least half the State Legislatures. Clause (c) covers 'any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule', which takes in List I, the Union List — so I qualifies. Clause (a) names Article 162 by number, and Article 162 is precisely 'Extent of the executive power of State' — so II qualifies. The conditions of the Governor's office are governed by Article 158, which appears nowhere in that proviso, so an amendment there needs only a special majority of Parliament — III does not qualify.

items.value: All three statements are correct
items.reasoning: Article 361(1) says the Governor shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office — statement I. Article 361(2) says no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the Governor in any court during his term of office — statement II, and the immunity is absolute for the term. Article 194(2) says no member of a State Legislature shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given in the Legislature or its committees — statement III.

items.value: Only two — refining, storage and distribution of petroleum, and marketing and sale of petroleum products
items.reasoning: The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006 gives the Board jurisdiction over the DOWNSTREAM chain: refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing and sale of petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas. Activities II and III fall squarely within that. Both upstream activities are expressly outside the Board's remit — the Act excludes production of crude oil and production of natural gas, which remain with the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas and the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons. So I and IV are not regulated by PNGRB.

items.value: All three are correct — revenue deficit ₹20,000 crore, fiscal deficit ₹10,000 crore, primary deficit ₹4,000 crore
items.reasoning: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts = 80,000 − 60,000 = ₹20,000 crore, so I holds. Fiscal deficit equals the government's total borrowing requirement, and the budget shows borrowings of ₹10,000 crore, so II holds. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 10,000 − 6,000 = ₹4,000 crore, so III holds. Worth noting for the student that a revenue deficit larger than the fiscal deficit is economically odd — it would imply large non-debt capital receipts — but the question asks only whether each figure follows from the data given, and all three do.

items.value: India to Central Asia to Europe via Iran
items.reasoning: The INSTC, launched in 2000 by its three founding members India, Iran and Russia, is a roughly 7,200 km ship-rail-road network running from India across the Arabian Sea to Iranian ports, then north through Iran to the Caspian and on to Russia, Central Asia and northern Europe. Iran is the indispensable transit node, which option A names. Option B is wrong because the corridor deliberately bypasses China; option C describes the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, not the INSTC. Option D is the weaker of the two plausible choices: Azerbaijan lies on only the western branch and the option omits Iran altogether, so A is the better description of what the corridor connects.

items.value: Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct — the USA, not Brazil, is the larger ethanol producer, and the feedstock contrast (corn versus sugarcane) is accurate
items.reasoning: Statement I inverts the ranking: the United States is the world's largest ethanol producer at roughly 15 billion gallons a year, well ahead of Brazil at roughly 8 to 9 billion gallons, so it is not true that Brazil produces more than the USA. Statement II is accurate: American ethanol is overwhelmingly made from corn, while Brazil's is made from sugarcane, which is why Brazilian ethanol has the better energy balance. Since Statement I is false, no option asserting both correct can stand, and D is the only remaining fit.

items.value: Statement II only — at a wet-bulb temperature of 35 °C the body can no longer shed heat by evaporation of sweat, threatening survival
items.reasoning: The wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature reachable by evaporative cooling at the prevailing humidity. Once it approaches 35 °C, sweat can no longer evaporate fast enough to carry away metabolic heat, so a healthy person cannot cool down even at rest in the shade — this is exactly the implication statement II states, and it applies to other mammals too. Statement I lists flooding, tropical cyclones and droughts, which are consequences of changed rainfall and ocean-heat patterns; they may well occur under climate change, but they are not what a routinely exceeded 35 °C wet-bulb threshold implies, so I does not reflect the report's finding.

items.value: ₹ 48,500 crores
items.reasoning: Gross primary deficit = gross fiscal deficit − interest payments = 50,000 − 1,500 = ₹48,500 crore. The ₹10,000 crore of non-debt creating capital receipts is a distractor: such receipts (disinvestment proceeds, recovery of loans) are already netted off in arriving at the fiscal deficit, so subtracting them again would be double counting — that error produces option C, ₹58,500 crore, if added instead. Option B, ₹51,500 crore, comes from adding the interest liability rather than subtracting it.

items.value: Statements I, III and IV are correct; the devolution share recommended was 41 per cent, not 45 per cent
items.reasoning: Statement II is decisive and it is false: the Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended that 41 per cent of the net proceeds of Union taxes be devolved to the States for 2021-26 (down from the 14th Commission's 42 per cent, the one-percentage-point adjustment being made for the newly formed Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh). Since every other option contains statement II, C is the only one that can stand. Independently, I is correct — ₹4,800 crore over 2022-23 to 2025-26 as a performance incentive for educational outcomes; III is correct — ₹45,000 crore as a performance-based incentive available to all States for agricultural reforms; and IV is correct — the Commission brought back a 'tax and fiscal efforts' criterion, with a 2.5 per cent weight, which the previous Commission had dropped.

items.value: Statements I and III only — IBRD lends to middle-income countries and was founded to rebuild post-war Europe, but it does not work single-handedly
items.reasoning: Statement I is correct: the IBRD's stated business is lending, guarantees, risk-management products and advisory services to middle-income and creditworthy low-income governments. Statement III is correct: the IBRD was created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and its first loans financed the reconstruction of war-damaged Europe, the development mandate coming later. Statement II fails on the word 'single-handedly': the IBRD is one of five institutions of the World Bank Group and the poverty mandate is shared, most directly with the IDA, which is the arm that lends concessionally to the poorest countries.

items.value: Statement I only — RTGS settles in real time and NEFT in batches, but inward transactions are free in both and both now operate round the clock
items.reasoning: Statement I is correct: RTGS settles each transaction individually and continuously in real time, whereas NEFT settles in deferred half-hourly batches, so an NEFT credit takes some time. Statement II is wrong: the RBI has always required that inward RTGS transactions carry no charge at the destination branch; charges, where levied, attach to outward transactions, and the same is true of NEFT. Statement III is wrong on current facts: NEFT has been available 24x7x365 since December 2019 and RTGS since December 2020, so neither has restricted operating hours and the contrast the statement draws no longer exists.

items.value: Only three — the United Arab Emirates, France and Singapore
items.reasoning: UPI merchant acceptance has been enabled in the UAE (through the NEOPAY network and partner banks), in France (through the Lyra network, beginning with the Eiffel Tower and e-commerce merchants), and in Singapore (through NPCI International's tie-up enabling UPI QR acceptance at merchants, alongside the separate UPI-PayNow remittance linkage). Germany has no UPI merchant acceptance arrangement, and Bangladesh has not gone live with one either, so both are out. That leaves three of the five listed countries.

items.value: All three statements are correct
items.reasoning: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, approved in February 2024 with an outlay of about ₹75,021 crore, targets rooftop solar installation in one crore households, which is statement I. Its capacity-building component tasks the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy with training in installation, operation, maintenance and repair of rooftop solar systems down to the grassroots level, which is statement II. The same component projects the creation of more than three lakh skilled personnel through fresh skilling and up-skilling, which is statement III. The scheme also provides direct central financial assistance, incentives to DISCOMs and a payment security mechanism.

items.value: At the time of publicly violating the Salt Law at Dandi
items.reasoning: The remark belongs with Gandhiji's open, deliberate law-breaking during the Civil Disobedience Movement, where he described British rule as a curse, said he was out to destroy that system of government, and framed his defiance as an avowedly seditious but non-violent duty — the salt-law breach at Dandi in April 1930 is that moment. Champaran (1917) is far too early, and there his plea was obedience to a higher law rather than sedition; at the Second Round Table Conference he was negotiating within the imperial framework; and his Quit India address of August 1942 is remembered for the 'Do or Die' mantra rather than this line. Flagged as low confidence: the phrasing is also sometimes placed at the 1922 Great Trial, where he said preaching disaffection had become 'almost a passion' with him, and that occasion is not among the options — so the letter rests on judgement about which listed event the quotation is associated with.

items.value: Bronze
items.reasoning: The 'Dancing Girl' from Mohenjo-daro is a roughly 10.5 cm bronze figurine cast by the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique, one of the best-known demonstrations that Harappan metalworkers had mastered copper-tin alloying and hollow casting. Carnelian was used in the Harappan world for beads, terracotta or clay for figurines and toys, and gold for ornaments, but none of these is the material of this particular statuette.

items.value: Madan Mohan Malaviya (with an associate) provided the legal defence
items.reasoning: Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, himself a lawyer, took up the defence of the villagers prosecuted after the Chauri Chaura incident of February 1922, appearing without fee in the appeal before the Allahabad High Court, where the great majority of the death sentences passed by the Sessions Court were set aside or commuted. None of the other names is associated with this case: C. R. Das had given up practice and was leading Non-Cooperation in Bengal, Saifuddin Kitchlew and Khwaja Hasan Nizami are linked with Punjab and Delhi politics respectively, and M. A. Jinnah had left the Congress by 1920. The second name printed alongside Malaviya could not be independently confirmed, which is why this is not marked high, but the option is the only defensible one.

items.value: The Poona Pact
items.reasoning: Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award of August 1932 gave the Depressed Classes separate electorates; Gandhiji began a fast unto death in Yerwada jail against it, and the deadlock was resolved by the Poona Pact of September 1932 with Dr B. R. Ambedkar, which substituted reserved seats within a joint electorate. Immediately afterwards Gandhiji made the removal of untouchability a central plank of his programme — founding the All India Anti-Untouchability League, soon renamed the Harijan Sevak Sangh, starting the weekly Harijan in 1933, and undertaking the Harijan tour of 1933-34. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) concerned suspension of Civil Disobedience, and options C and D are later and unrelated.

items.value: All the three — papaya, pineapple and guava were Portuguese introductions
items.reasoning: All three are New World plants that reached India through the Portuguese in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: papaya and guava from Central America and pineapple from tropical South America. They belong to the same set of Portuguese introductions as the cashew, custard apple, chilli, potato and tobacco, a point historians of the Mughal economy make when noting how the Indian fruit basket changed in that period. None of the three is native to India or attested in Indian sources before the Portuguese arrival.
